title: Design patterns I: creational
problem: Code that builds its own collaborators with new cannot be tested, grows an if-chain for every new type, and leaks constructor details into every caller.
summary: Creational patterns separate deciding which object to build from using it: Factory Method centralises the choice, Abstract Factory keeps families consistent, Builder assembles objects with many optional parts, and Singleton's global access is the part to avoid.
catTip: I am an instance of Cat, built by a Builder: whiskers, tail and appetite set step by step, validated once. Please do not make me a Singleton; the test suite needs a fresh cat.

recall.q: A checkout needs a charger, a refunder and a webhook verifier that must all belong to the same payment provider. Which creational pattern fits, and why not a plain factory method?
recall.a: Abstract Factory: one interface with a creation method per family member and one concrete factory per provider, so the client can never mix a Razorpay charger with a Stripe refunder. A single factory method returns one product and cannot enforce that several products match.

guide.breaks: Without a creational pattern the class that uses an object also decides its concrete type, so every new type edits working code and no test can substitute a fake.
guide.tradeoffs: Every pattern adds at least one interface and one class, and a Singleton's convenient global access hides dependencies and makes tests order-dependent.
guide.explainSimply: Instead of making every part of a program build the things it needs, you hand the building to a specialist. It is like ordering at a restaurant counter: you say what you want, and the kitchen decides who cooks it and how. The program only has to know what it asked for.
guide.hint: Think about what must stay consistent across several objects, not just how one object gets created.

meow: Meow-ke me with a Builder, pick my food with a Factory, and never, ever getInstance() the cat.

quiz.prompt: A class has a constructor with nine parameters, five of which are optional and two of which must never be combined. Which pattern addresses this most directly?
quiz.explanation: A Builder names each optional part at the call site and validates the combination once in build(). Abstract Factory is about producing a consistent family of different objects, not about assembling one object with many options.

quiz.prompt: Why do experienced reviewers treat a Singleton accessed through getInstance() as a design smell?
options: Java cannot guarantee a single instance, so the pattern never works
It is slower than creating a new object on every call
Every caller gains a hidden dependency that tests cannot replace, and shared state leaks between tests
It prevents the class from implementing an interface
quiz.explanation: The problem is global access, not the single instance: constructors stop declaring what they need and tests cannot swap in a fake. Java can guarantee one instance per JVM (an enum singleton does), so the first option is wrong.

cards.q: A teammate replaces every new SmtpSender() with SmtpSender.getInstance(). What did they fix, and what did they break?
cards.a: They removed duplicated construction and kept a single instance, but they hid the dependency: callers no longer declare it, tests cannot substitute a fake, and state is shared across tests. Build the instance once at the composition root and inject it instead.

cards.q: Factory Method and Abstract Factory in one sentence each?
cards.a: Factory Method returns one product behind an interface so the concrete class is chosen in one place. Abstract Factory returns a family of related products from one concrete factory so they are guaranteed to match.

glossary.note: Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides, authors of Design Patterns (1994); their 23 patterns are the ones interviewers name.
